result.text:
## What are you actually choosing together?
A lot of romantic pain starts with two lovey bunnies entering one of the biggest arrangements of their lives without ever discussing their ideas, dreams, and fears about it.
“We’re together” ... what does that mean exactly? It conjures up for me thoughts of romance, sex, exclusivity, living together, shared money, children, caregiving, spiritual partnership, family identity, or just “we really like each other and we’ll see.” Lack of specificity is sometimes a nice way to flow, but the problem is that each person could be imagining a different bundle from those pieces, then either not labeling anything or assuming one relationship label settled it.
Wanting somebody doesn't tell me whether I should have children with her or build a life with her. One of the stupid things my brain can do is turn “I'm taking a chance on her” into “she's the right person” after we've been together for a while. Based on what? Sometimes I actually learned something. Sometimes nothing changed except that now I'm attached, and the new certainty is just harder for me to question.
One honest option is basically a "practical partnership." This is very common, especially outside the modern West. Two people may share a home, raise children, support each other financially, take care of each other, and maybe have sex, without pretending the whole thing rests on overwhelming romantic love.
Although this feels wrong to me and anyone else who has been in love, arguably, there is nothing inherently wrong with that if both people know that’s what they are doing. This arrangement has been promoted throughout history because it isn't based on highly fluctuating feelings, but ironically, that's also what can make it unstable. Imagine you're in this, and then one day you find your heartthrob at work or church or somewhere else, and suddenly you wonder why you ever settled for less.
Another honest option is a romance with humility, even if it seems to clash. Two people really are in love, really do want to build something together, and really do take the bond seriously, but they do not pretend they can guarantee the feeling forever.
They can still choose exclusivity, shack up, have children, and plan a life. The honest part is that they admit feelings can change, and they talk beforehand about what that would mean. If the romance fades, maybe they revive it, or maybe they renegotiate the arrangement.
My actual ideal is to have intimacy embedded in community.
One of the best reasons for that is because romance often ceases to be romance when it's bogged down by practical daily survival. Once the same person has to be your lover, your family, your whole social world, your housing security, your therapist, your emergency contact, and your entire future, it becomes very hard to appreciate the romance for its own sake. Every romantic problem now threatens the rest of your life too, which makes it hard to open your heart deeply.
If people are supported by a wider field, then romance does not have to hold the whole roof up by itself. Dyads can still be very important, but they are not carrying every human need alone.
Obviously most people are not going to live in a free-love community unless we really have a New Earth soon. But, as Pema Chodron says to prisoners when teaching them meditation, "Start Where You Are." Build mutual friendships, and keep other sources of meaning and support alive. Try not to structure your whole life so that if the romance changes, everything else collapses too.
These are just a few options I could think of to start the ball rolling, but be creative and see what you come up with!
Before you commit to one type of relationship, ask each other some real questions:
What are we deciding to join together, and why?
Is this mainly a romance, a practical partnership, or both?
Are we promising actions, or quietly pretending to promise permanent feelings?
If the romance changes, which parts of this agreement still remain?
And the biggie: what happens if one of us falls in love with someone else?
What counts as betrayal, and what just means we need a serious conversation?
Which needs should still be supported mostly outside the relationship?
How should we plan on revisiting this agreement when our lives change?
If we separate, what do we still owe each other, and what do we owe any children involved?
You can make a card game out of this and have some fun with it. If there's real love, it will survive a bit of honest curiosity.
